files.lesson.md: --- order: 11 unit: solids node: [AC9M7SP01 n2, AC9M7SP01 n3] title: Views of a solid summary: "A pile of cubes can be drawn in 3D or as top, front and side views. A front or side view shows only the tallest pile in each column; a top view with numbers shows every pile." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "An architect shows a building from above, from the front and from the side. Why not just one drawing?" connection: floor-plan app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8296 url: http://127.0.0.1:8296/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: views.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Three drawings of the same cubes: top, front and side. The tall pile hides the one behind it." } explainClip: query: { code: "@views.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Build, then look" say: "Add cubes and watch the three views change." clip: - caption: { text: "An empty base. Add cubes at the front.", say: "An empty base. Add cubes at the front." } - click: "Row 3 (front), column 1: 0 cubes. Press to add one." - click: "Row 3 (front), column 1: 1 cube. Press to add one." - click: "Row 3 (front), column 2: 0 cubes. Press to add one." - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "3 cubes: top 2 squares, front 3, side 2" } - wait: 1500 - caption: { text: "A tower of 2 and a single cube: the front view has 3 squares.", say: "A tower of two and a single cube. The front view has three squares." } - wait: 1200 --- An **isometric drawing** shows a solid in 3D on isometric (triangle) paper. **Views** are flat drawings seen from one side: the **top** view (also called the plan), the **front** view and the **side** view (together called elevations). A view shows what you can see; cubes hidden behind others do not show. ## Predict: one view ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to whether the front view gives the number of cubes shows whether they know a view hides cubes." check: type: predict q: "You see only the front view of a pile of cubes. Can you tell how many cubes there are?" options: ["No: cubes behind the front ones do not show", "Yes: count the squares", "Only if you also know the side view"] actual: "No. A front view shows the tallest pile in each column; cubes behind it, or lower down, are hidden." ``` Picture a tall tower with a short pile directly behind it. ## Run: three views ```step stage: run insight: "Changing cubes and watching the three views shows what each view reveals and what it hides." try: { playground: board, starter: "views.yml#run", height: 650 } check: { type: board, text: "Change the piles so the top view has 4 squares and the front view has 5. Which piles did you change?", when: "t = 4 and f = 5", explain: "The top view counts the occupied cells; the front view counts, for each column, only the tallest pile." } ``` Press a cell in the grid to add a cube to that pile. After the tallest, it goes back to 0. ## Investigate: what a view shows ```step stage: investigate insight: "A view shows only the tallest pile in each column (Noor adds the piles); the top view with numbers shows the most." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A column has piles of 3, 1 and 2 cubes, one behind another. How many squares does the front view show for that column?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["6", "The front view shows only the tallest pile. The lower piles are hidden behind it."] explain: "The tallest pile is 3, so the front view shows 3 squares for that column." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#noor" text: "Noor works out the front view of a column of piles. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: view-adds-up explain: "Line 3: a front view shows only the tallest pile in each column, not all of them added up." - check: type: question q: "Which drawing tells you exactly how many cubes there are?" options: ["A top view with the height written on each pile", "The front view", "The side view", "The top view with no numbers"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "It hides the piles behind the front ones.", "It hides the piles behind the nearest ones.", "It shows which cells have cubes, not how tall the piles are."] explain: "With a height on every pile, adding the numbers gives the total." ``` ### Hidden cubes How tall is the tallest pile? ### Find the mistake Read Noor's working. What does the view show? ### Which drawing ## Modify: build to a description ```step stage: modify insight: "Building to a description uses the views to reason about hidden cubes: the fewest, the most, and the trade-offs of each drawing." try: { playground: board, starter: "views.yml#free", height: 650 } tasks: - starter: "views.yml#free" hint: ["Piles of 1 cube only.", "Use six of the nine cells, with at least one in every row and every column."] check: { type: board, text: "Build a shape with 6 cubes whose front view and side view each have 3 squares.", when: "n = 6 and f = 3 and s = 3", explain: "Six piles of one cube spread over the 3 by 3 base, with every row and every column used, give 3 squares in the front view and 3 in the side view." } smaller: check: { type: number, q: "The front view shows 3 squares in a row, all one cube tall. How many of the 3 columns must have at least one cube in them?", answer: 3, tolerance: 0, explain: "A square in the front view comes from a column with a cube in it. 3 squares means all 3 columns." } - starter: "views.yml#free" check: { type: board, text: "Build the fewest cubes that give a top view of 4 squares.", when: "n = 4 and t = 4", explain: "Each square of the top view needs at least one cube, so the fewest is 4." } - starter: "views.yml#free" hint: ["The top view has 4 squares, so 4 piles.", "The tallest pile is 3, so every pile can be at most 3."] check: { type: board, text: "Build the most cubes you can with a top view of 4 squares and no pile taller than 3.", when: "n = 12 and t = 4 and h = 3", explain: "4 piles of 3 cubes make 12." } - starter: "views.yml#top" hint: ["Press a cell until its number matches.", "The numbers are back row 2 1 0, middle row 0 3 0, front row 0 0 1."] check: { type: board, text: "The top view of a solid has these heights. Back row: 2, 1, 0. Middle row: 0, 3, 0. Front row: 0, 0, 1. Build it. How many cubes?", when: "n = 7 and t = 4 and f = 6", explain: "2 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 7 cubes. The front view shows the tallest pile in each column: 2, 3 and 1, so 6 squares." } - check: type: question q: "What is one advantage of a net over a 3D drawing?" options: ["It shows every face at its true size, so you can find the surface area", "It shows what the solid looks like from the front", "It is quicker to draw", "It shows the height of every pile"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is a view.", "A net takes care to draw.", "That is a top view with numbers."] explain: "A net lays every face flat, true size; a 3D drawing shows what the solid looks like but squashes the faces." ``` ### Six cubes Both views must be 3 squares. ### The fewest ### The most ### From a top view ### Nets or drawings ## Practise: views ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading views and counting cubes, mixed; adding the piles is the planted slip; the cube net review keeps nets fresh." try: { playground: board, starter: "views.yml#side", height: 600 } tasks: - starter: "views.yml#side" check: type: answer q: "Look at the stack on the board. How many squares does its side view show?" answer: "3" feedback: - ["4", "That is the front view. The side view is seen from the right."] explain: "From the right, the rows give tallest piles 2, 0 and 1: 3 squares." - check: type: answer q: "A top view with heights is 3 1 on the top row and 0 2 on the bottom row. How many cubes are there?" answer: "6" feedback: - ["4", "That counts the squares. Add the heights: 3 + 1 + 0 + 2."] explain: "3 + 1 + 0 + 2 = 6 cubes." - check: type: question q: "Which view shows which cells of the base have cubes?" options: ["The top view", "The front view", "The side view", "The isometric drawing"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The front view shows the heights of the columns seen from the front.", "The side view shows the heights from the right.", "It shows them, but in 3D, and hides some."] explain: "Looking down, the top view shows a square for every occupied cell." - check: type: question q: "Review: which of these six-square nets folds into a cube?" options: ["A cross: one square above and one below a row of four", "A 2 by 3 block", "A straight row of six", "A row of three above a row of three"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Two squares land on the same face.", "The row wraps back on itself.", "Two squares land on the same face."] explain: "Only the cross-shaped net covers all six faces once." ``` ### Side view ### Cube count ### The top view ### Review: nets ## Make: two designs ```step stage: make insight: "Building a solid whose three views match, then judging nets against drawings, brings the lesson's representations together." try: { playground: board, starter: "views.yml#free", height: 650 } hint: ["A top view of 5 squares needs 5 piles.", "Some piles must be 2 cubes tall, or the front and side views are too small."] check: { type: board, text: "Build a solid whose top, front and side views each have 5 squares.", when: "t = 5 and f = 5 and s = 5", explain: "One answer, rows from back to front: 0 0 1, then 0 0 2, then 1 2 1. Five occupied cells; the tallest pile in each column adds to 5, and in each row to 5." } ``` Write one advantage and one disadvantage of nets and of 3D drawings. ## Make: a bedroom plan, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A floor plan is the view from above: it shows lengths and widths to scale and hides heights, so another view is needed for them." hint: ["What is a floor plan the view from?", "What can't you see when you look straight down?"] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Sam checks a bedroom's floor plan, drawn from above to scale, to see whether a bed and a desk fit and the door can open. They do. Then she buys a tall bookcase, and it hits the sloping ceiling. On paper, say what the plan shows, what it hides, and which view would have shown the problem." steps: - ["A plan is the top view: it shows lengths and widths of the floor", "so Sam could place the bed, desk and door swing to scale"] - ["It cannot show how tall things are", "heights are hidden when you look straight down"] - ["The ceiling slope shows in a front or side view", "those views show heights"] picks: - step: 1 q: "What does a view from above not show?" options: - "How tall things are" - "How long things are" - "How wide things are" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The plan shows lengths. It is heights that are hidden.", "The plan shows widths. It is heights that are hidden."] - step: 3 q: "Which view would have shown the sloping ceiling?" options: - "A front or side view, which shows heights" - "A second plan from above" - "A bigger plan from above" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Another view from above still cannot show heights.", "Making the plan bigger does not change what it hides."] criteria: - "I said the plan is the top view and what it shows." - "I said what it hides: heights." - "I named a view that shows the sloping ceiling." explain: "A plan shows lengths and widths, so the bed, desk and door could be placed. It hides heights, so only a front or side view shows the sloping ceiling." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Sam and her room are made up, but plans really hide heights. Write what the plan shows, what it hides and which view fills the gap, then choose the reasons that matter most. **Also used in** - **Architects and builders.** Plans, front and side views are drawn together because each hides what the others show. - **Packing and shipping.** A box must fit in all three directions, so you check length, width and height, not only the floor space. ```teacher summary: Students build piles of cubes and compare the isometric drawing with the top, front and side views, finding what each view hides (AC9M7SP01, nodes 2 and 3). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can draw or read the top, front and side views of a pile of cubes. - I can say what a view hides. - I can say one advantage and one disadvantage of a net and of a 3D drawing. struggle: Knowing which side is which. Turn a real pile of cubes round on the desk beside the board; the side view is seen from the right. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Build a small pile from linking cubes to hold up. The one idea: a view shows only what you can see from one side, so the front and side views show the tallest pile in each column and hide the rest. The common mistake is adding the piles (Noor's mistake). The board's rows run from the back (top of the grid) to the front. The front view looks from the front; the side view looks from the right. The top view puts the back row at the top. The view orientation is the hinge for this node: students who mix up front and side cannot compare representations. running: - "Predict: ask what could be hiding behind the front pile." - "Run: ask students to say which view they think will change before they press." - "Investigate: ask Noor's question again with a column of 1, 3, 1." - "Modify: ask for the fewest cubes first, then the most." - "Make: ask which drawing they would give a builder." - "Paper: the bedroom-plan task is worked in books; the page marks two reasons (what a plan hides, and which view shows the slope). Books out, then look at the page to compare the three lines." stuck: - see: A student adds all the piles to find a view. ask: If you stand at the front, which cubes can you see in one column? fix: Only the tallest pile. Lower piles are hidden behind it. - see: A student confuses front and side views. ask: Which way are you looking? Which row is nearest you? fix: Front looks from the front row; side looks from the right. - see: A student thinks the isometric drawing shows every cube. ask: Can you see the cube hidden behind the tall pile? fix: No drawing from one direction shows everything; the top view with numbers is the exception. stretch: Two different piles can have the same top, front and side views. Can you find a pair? support: Use a real pile of linking cubes and look at it from each side before using the board. leads: > This completes AC9M7SP01. Where it leads: building solids from their views, and surface area and volume of prisms (Measurement); drawing in perspective in Year 8. exit: q: A front view shows 3 squares. Does the pile have 3 cubes? Why or why not? a: Not necessarily. The front view shows only the tallest pile in each column; there could be more cubes behind. explain: > A **view** is what you see from one side. The **top** view (plan) looks down; the **front** and **side** views (elevations) look across. They show the tallest pile in each column, and hide cubes behind or beneath. A top view with a number on each pile shows every cube. A **net** shows every face at its true size, but not what the solid looks like when built. ```
